scholars.name_en: Banu Musa (the sons of Musa ibn Shakir)
scholars.biography: The Banū Mūsā were three brothers—Muḥammad, Aḥmad, and Ḥasan, sons of Mūsā ibn Shākir—active in ninth-century Baghdad. Pingree describes their upbringing and scientific activity there; Casulleras cautions that the surviving record does not support separate full biographies. Their shared patronage of translation and research is summarized in the cited group contribution, without assigning every commission or work to one brother.

scholars.name_en: Muhammad ibn Musa ibn Shakir (of the Banu Musa)
scholars.dates: born early 9th century – January or February 873
scholars.dates_note: born at the beginning of the 9th century; died January or February 873

claims.text: His origin is uncertain: the epithet al-Khwarizmi suggests Khwarizm (south of the Aral Sea), Ibn al-Nadim says he came from there, but al-Tabari also calls him al-Qutrubbulli (a district near Baghdad); DSB suggests his ancestors, not he, may have come from Khwarizm.
claims.label: DISPUTED
claims.note: Both sources say the evidence is mixed.

claims.text: His religion is read differently: DSB takes al-Tabari's epithet al-Majusi to mean at most Zoroastrian forebears (the pious preface of the Algebra shows an orthodox Muslim), while BEA reads the epithet as indicating a Zoroastrian rather than a Muslim.
claims.label: DISPUTED
claims.note: The two sources differ.

claims.text: He worked in Baghdad in close connection with the Abbasid court, especially under Caliph al-Ma'mun (reigned 813–833).
claims.label: VERIFIED

sources.locator: entry: House of Wisdom and al-Ma'mun

claims.note: Both read sources agree.

claims.text: DSB says he became a member of the House of Wisdom under al-Ma'mun; BEA reports that Ibn al-Nadim attaches him to it but notes considerable modern controversy over what the institution was (library, or translation and research institution).
claims.label: ACADEMICALLY SUPPORTED

sources.locator: entry: House of Wisdom and al-Ma'mun

claims.note: Membership rests on a medieval report; the institution's nature is disputed.

claims.text: His dates are approximate: BEA gives born c. 780 and died c. 850; DSB gives born before 800 and died after 847.
claims.label: ACADEMICALLY SUPPORTED
claims.note: The two are compatible but differ in precision. No exact dates are known.

claims.text: Reports that he went on a mission to the Khazars, or took part in a geodetic expedition, are disputed: DSB thinks the Khazar and Seven Sleepers envoy was probably the Banu Musa's Muhammad; BEA says he may have joined expeditions but doubts the first has been raised (King 2000).
claims.label: DISPUTED
claims.note: Possible confusion with a Banu Musa brother (see B-01).

claims.text: He dedicated his Algebra and his astronomical work (the zij) to al-Ma'mun.
claims.label: VERIFIED

claims.text: Surviving and lost works: the Algebra survives in Arabic; the Hindu-numerals arithmetic is lost in Arabic but survives in Latin; the original zij is lost in Arabic and survives only in Latin versions of later revisions; the Geography and a Jewish-calendar treatise survive in Arabic; a Chronicle is lost but quoted by historians.
claims.label: VERIFIED
claims.note: Both read sources agree on survival status.

claims.text: The Algebra, al-Kitab al-mukhtasar fi hisab al-jabr wa'l-muqabala ('The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing'), treats equations of the first and second degree (reduced to six standard forms by 'completion' and 'balancing'), then mensuration, commercial problems and inheritance problems.
claims.label: VERIFIED
claims.note: Described as practical mathematics, not an abstract treatise.

claims.text: The Algebra uses no symbols (even for numerals): everything is written out in words, with shay' ('thing'), mal (square) and jidhr (root).
claims.label: ACADEMICALLY SUPPORTED
claims.note: Single source among those read.

claims.text: His Algebra is the first known (reported) work on algebra written in Arabic. This does not make it the first algebra anywhere: DSB stresses that Greek and Hindu algebra had already advanced further.
claims.label: ACADEMICALLY SUPPORTED
claims.note: DSB says 'we are told' it was the first in Arabic: a report, not a proven fact.

claims.text: Where his algebraic methods came from is disputed: arguments for Hindu sources (rhetorical style, rule of three, circle formulas) and for Greek geometry (Euclid II); a closely related Hebrew treatise, Mishnat ha-Middot, is dated either c. 150 CE (Gandz) or to an early Islamic period (Sarfatti), so the direction of borrowing is unsettled.
claims.label: DISPUTED
claims.note: Reported as an open scholarly dispute.

claims.text: His treatise on Hindu numerals (Arabic title uncertain) expounds the digits 1–9, zero and place value; DSB thinks it likely that the decimal place-value system was a recent arrival from India and that his work was the first to expound it systematically, noting the Latin text is probably much altered.
claims.label: ACADEMICALLY SUPPORTED
claims.note: Hedged in the source ('likely enough'). Not a claim that he invented the numerals.

claims.text: The Algebra was translated into Latin by at least two translators and strongly influenced elementary algebra in Arabic, Persian, Ottoman Turkish, Latin and European vernaculars.
claims.label: VERIFIED

claims.text: DSB names Robert of Chester and Gerard of Cremona as the 12th-century Latin translators of the algebraic part; it notes the attribution to Gerard is complicated by a free adaptation also ascribed to him. The Latin Hindu-numerals text (early 12th century) led to 'algorismus' and the word 'algorithm'.
claims.label: ACADEMICALLY SUPPORTED
claims.note: Single source.

claims.text: His zij is a revision in the Zij al-Sindhind tradition, mixing Indian (Hindu) parameters and methods, Sasanian elements and Ptolemaic material.
claims.label: VERIFIED
claims.note: Specifics differ in emphasis between the sources.

claims.text: The sources disagree on observations in the zij: DSB finds no trace of original observation in the extant tables (while noting the lost original introduction reportedly discussed Baghdad observations under al-Ma'mun giving an obliquity of 23°33′), whereas BEA says the tables include values determined by observations during al-Ma'mun's reign.
claims.label: DISPUTED
claims.note: Preserved as a disagreement.

claims.text: No Arabic copy of his zij survives; it is known through Latin translation (probably by Adelard of Bath, early 12th century) of the revision by Maslama al-Majriti (d. 1007–08), and through the Toledan Tables. Later astronomers including al-Farghani and al-Biruni commented on it.
claims.label: VERIFIED
claims.note: Commentators noted for relationships in Sub-batch 2B/2C.

claims.text: His Geography, Kitab surat al-ard, is mostly lists of coordinates arranged by climate zone; it is related to Ptolemy's Geography but not a translation of it, and DSB reports it is more accurate in areas ruled by Islam (notably a shorter Mediterranean) and introduces errors of its own. A derivation from a map, possibly al-Ma'mun's, is a scholar's conjecture.
claims.label: ACADEMICALLY SUPPORTED
claims.note: DSB adds that it was unknown in Europe until the late 19th century.

claims.text: His Jewish-calendar treatise dates to no earlier than 823/824 (it carries an example for that year).
claims.label: VERIFIED

claims.text: His astrolabe writings survive only fragmentarily and scholars differ on whether the fragments are genuine; DSB thinks the content was probably drawn from earlier works.
claims.label: DISPUTED

claims.text: DSB's judgement is that his scientific achievements were modest but extremely influential, because they transmitted Indian and Greek knowledge at a favorable time; BEA stresses the substantial influence of the Algebra. Other scholars' rankings differ (see lead L-MT, not read).
claims.label: ACADEMICALLY SUPPORTED
claims.note: An evaluation by the entry's author, recorded as such.

claims.text: The Banu Musa were three sons of Musa ibn Shakir: (Jafar) Muhammad (died January or February 873), Abu al-Qasim Ahmad and al-Hasan (both died in the 9th century); all born in Baghdad at the start of the 9th century. BEA says separate biographies are quite impossible.
claims.label: ACADEMICALLY SUPPORTED
claims.note: One source. Not to be confused with al-Khwarizmi, whom some reports call 'Muhammad ibn Musa the astronomer' (see K-06).

claims.text: Their father Musa ibn Shakir is described as a reformed bandit who became an astronomer or astrologer and a friend of al-Ma'mun; after his death al-Ma'mun became guardian of the brothers and sent them to the House of Wisdom.
claims.label: UNDER REVIEW
claims.note: BEA says 'is described as': biographical tradition, unchecked.

claims.text: They worked with al-Ma'mun and his successors on geodetic surveys and on contracting public works, became wealthy, and used part of their wealth to sponsor scientific research and translation.
claims.label: ACADEMICALLY SUPPORTED

claims.text: They obtained classical manuscripts from Byzantium by sending agents or travelling; on one trip Muhammad met Thabit ibn Qurra of Harran and brought him to Baghdad, where he joined their circle; Hunayn ibn Ishaq is described as part of their team.
claims.label: ACADEMICALLY SUPPORTED
claims.note: Relationships with Thabit and Hunayn to be recorded in Sub-batch 2B.

claims.text: About 20 books are known under the Banu Musa on astronomy, mechanics and mathematics; the majority of the astronomical works are lost.
claims.label: ACADEMICALLY SUPPORTED
claims.note: Count as stated in BEA-BM.

claims.text: Muhammad's works include On the Visibility of the Crescent, a Book on the Beginning of the World, and a book variously titled on the motion of the celestial spheres / astronomy, which criticises the Ptolemaic system by explaining daily motion through rotation of all spheres and denying a ninth sphere.
claims.label: ACADEMICALLY SUPPORTED

claims.text: Ahmad is reportedly the author of a geometric proof that there is no ninth sphere, texts on questions discussed with Sanad ibn 'Ali, a zij mentioned by Ibn Yunus (who also mentions a zij by the three brothers), and a Reasoning on the Trisection of an Angle.
claims.label: ACADEMICALLY SUPPORTED
claims.note: BEA words these as 'reportedly'.

claims.text: The Book on the Solar Year was traditionally attributed to Thabit ibn Qurra, but recent research cited by BEA indicates it is most likely a misattribution and the work of the Banu Musa.
claims.label: ATTRIBUTION UNCERTAIN
claims.note: Attribution moved by later research; one source.

claims.text: Their Book on the Measurement of Plane and Spherical Figures was recast by Nasir al-Din al-Tusi (13th century) and translated into Latin by Gerard of Cremona (12th century) as Liber trium fratrum de geometria and Verba filiorum Moysi filii Sekir; BEA says its contents appear in works by Thabit ibn Qurra, Ibn al-Haytham, Fibonacci, Jordanus de Nemore and Roger Bacon.
claims.label: ACADEMICALLY SUPPORTED
claims.note: Influence claims are BEA's, not independently checked.

claims.text: Other geometry works attributed to them include three books related to Apollonius' Conics, a book on a proposition proved by Galen, and a Book on an Oblong Round Figure, which concerns the ellipse and describes the string-and-pegs ('gardener's') construction.
claims.label: ACADEMICALLY SUPPORTED

claims.text: BEA says they produced major work in mechanics that marks significant advances over Philo of Byzantium and Hero of Alexandria, whose works Muslim engineers knew well; its reference list cites the Kitab al-Hiyal (ed. al-Hassan, Aleppo 1981) and Hill's 1979 translation.
claims.label: ACADEMICALLY SUPPORTED
claims.note: BEA does not describe individual devices here. Device-level claims need Hill (L-HILL).

claims.text: Popular pages claim about 100 devices, early gas masks, a 'first programmable machine', a date around 850 and a division of labor between the brothers (Ahmad in engineering) that BEA does not give (BEA assigns astronomy and geometry works to Ahmad).
claims.label: UNVERIFIED
claims.note: Not used as evidence. Verify against Hill's translation.

claims.text: Muhammad's son Nu'aym ibn Muhammad ibn Musa wrote a Book on Geometric Propositions, continuing the family tradition.
claims.label: ACADEMICALLY SUPPORTED

claims.text: Abu Yusuf Ya'qub ibn Ishaq al-Kindi belonged to the Arab tribe of Kinda (hence 'philosopher of the Arabs'); he was born in Basra and educated in Baghdad.
claims.label: ACADEMICALLY SUPPORTED
claims.note: Single source.

claims.text: His dates are approximate: he died after 866 CE, usually put in the early 870s; his birth date is harder to pin down and is usually reckoned as around 800, inferred from service under al-Ma'mun (reign ended 833) and association with al-Mu'tasim (reigned 833–842).
claims.label: ACADEMICALLY SUPPORTED
claims.note: Inference, not a recorded date.

claims.text: His career peaked under al-Mu'tasim, to whom he dedicated On First Philosophy and whose son Ahmad he tutored.
claims.label: ACADEMICALLY SUPPORTED

claims.text: He oversaw one of the two main groups of translators of the 9th century (the other led by Hunayn ibn Ishaq): the 'Kindi circle' rendered Greek philosophy and science into Arabic. He seems to have mediated between patrons and the translators, many of them Syrian Christians.
claims.label: ACADEMICALLY SUPPORTED
claims.note: The circle produced the Theology of Aristotle (SEP §2.1). Relationship to Hunayn for Sub-batch 2B.

claims.text: Ibn al-Nadim's Fihrist (10th century) lists works ascribed to him, hundreds of treatises, with scientific and mathematical titles outnumbering philosophical ones; many are lost, and a single manuscript held in Istanbul preserves most of his extant philosophical writings.
claims.label: ACADEMICALLY SUPPORTED
claims.note: No shelfmark is given in SEP-K, so none is recorded.

claims.text: On First Philosophy survives incomplete (first part, four sections); it argues the world is not eternal and God is a simple 'true One'. Its argument against eternity follows John Philoponus; SEP judges the argument weak and its success unclear.
claims.label: ACADEMICALLY SUPPORTED
claims.note: A synthesis of Greek arguments, not an independent invention.

claims.text: On the Intellect survives in Arabic (few copies) and Latin and is the first treatise in the Arabic tradition to give a taxonomy of types of intellect.
claims.label: ACADEMICALLY SUPPORTED

claims.text: His optics follows Euclid and Ptolemy (vision by rays emitted from the eye along straight lines) and criticises shortcomings in Euclid's optics; On Perspectives survives only in Latin. SEP says aspects of his account anticipate Ibn al-Haytham, who some decades later was first to explain vision accurately.
claims.label: ACADEMICALLY SUPPORTED
claims.note: Not an anticipation of modern optics: see M-Q1.

claims.text: On Rays (De radiis) survives only in Latin and its authenticity is disputed: a strong case against has been made (Matton 2022), while SEP says it may be partly based on authentic material.
claims.label: DISPUTED
claims.note: Do not credit al-Kindi with its theory without further evidence.

claims.text: He wrote many works on astrology, treating it as a rational science with a physical theory of astral causation, and cosmological treatises (e.g. On the Prostration of the Outermost Sphere); his astrology was the most influential part of his work for Latin authors.
claims.label: ACADEMICALLY SUPPORTED
claims.note: See M-Q2 for the modern assessment.

claims.text: His extant scientific corpus is sizable (drugs, music, astrology, mathematics); he applied mathematics, especially geometry, across fields, and optics and medicine are well represented.
claims.label: ACADEMICALLY SUPPORTED

claims.text: His thought draws on Aristotle (main authority), Neoplatonism (Proclus, Plotinus), Philoponus, and Greek mathematical authors such as Euclid and Nicomachus.
claims.label: ACADEMICALLY SUPPORTED

claims.text: Al-'Amiri was a second-generation student of his through Abu Zayd al-Balkhi; Isaac Israeli and Miskawayh were influenced by him; later Arabic authors rarely cite him after the 10th century, while Latin authors valued his astrology and some translated works.
claims.label: ACADEMICALLY SUPPORTED
claims.note: Persons not yet in the archive.

claims.text: On Definitions, ascribed to him, has doubted authenticity; it is almost certainly at least a product of his circle, composed in several strata.
claims.label: ATTRIBUTION UNCERTAIN

claims.text: SEP calls him the first self-identified philosopher in the Arabic tradition. This is the entry author's characterisation.
claims.label: ACADEMICALLY SUPPORTED
claims.note: Evaluative; not independently verified.

claims.text: Modern optics explains vision by light entering the eye, not by rays emitted from the eye; the emission model was superseded.
claims.label: MODERN SCIENTIFIC ASSESSMENT
claims.note: Drafted by ISA from standard knowledge; no citation yet.
claims.needs: Cite an optics or history-of-science reference.

claims.text: Astrology has no empirical support in modern science; ISA records it as part of the historical natural philosophy of the period.
claims.label: MODERN SCIENTIFIC ASSESSMENT
claims.note: Drafted by ISA; no citation yet.
claims.needs: Cite a history-of-science or astronomy reference.

claims.text: Modern astronomy does not use physical celestial spheres; the Banu Musa critique concerns the internal structure of the Ptolemaic cosmos and is a historical argument.
claims.label: MODERN SCIENTIFIC ASSESSMENT
claims.note: Drafted by ISA; no citation yet.

contributions.title: Algebra treatise: systematic reduction to standard forms
contributions.text: A compendium that reduces first- and second-degree problems to six standard forms using 'completion' (al-jabr) and 'balancing' (al-muqabala), with worked applications to mensuration, trade and inheritance, written entirely in words. Reported as the first known algebra work in Arabic.
contributions.prior: Greek and Hindu algebraic knowledge, which had advanced further in places but did not resemble this presentation (DSB).
contributions.detail: A practical, systematic handbook that fixed the terminology and form later Arabic algebra and Latin translations used. Not the first algebra, and the source of its methods is disputed (K-12).
contributions.label: under_review

contributions.title: Exposition of the Hindu numerals and place value
contributions.text: An arithmetic treatise using the digits 1–9, zero and the place-value system, preserved only in Latin; DSB thinks he was probably the first to expound the decimal system systematically in Arabic.
contributions.prior: The Hindu numerals and decimal place value reached Baghdad from India; alphabetic and sexagesimal systems were in use (DSB).
contributions.detail: A systematic exposition for Arabic readers. DSB hedges ('likely enough'); the Arabic original is lost and the Latin text may be altered. Not a claim that he invented the numerals.
contributions.label: under_review

contributions.title: Zij: revision of the Sindhind astronomical tradition
contributions.text: A set of astronomical tables and rules revising the Zij al-Sindhind, mixing Indian, Sasanian and Ptolemaic elements; the original is lost and known only through later revisions.
contributions.prior: Earlier Zij al-Sindhind handbooks (BEA names al-Fazari), the Zij al-Shah and Ptolemy's tables (DSB, BEA).
contributions.detail: A revision for al-Ma'mun that spread Indian astronomical methods and, via Latin, reached Europe. Whether it contains original observations is disputed (K-17).
contributions.label: under_review

contributions.title: Geography: coordinate tables of the known world
contributions.text: A list of latitudes and longitudes of places grouped by climate zone, related to but different from Ptolemy's Geography, with a shorter Mediterranean and errors of its own.
contributions.prior: Ptolemy's Geography and probably al-Ma'mun's world map (a conjecture, DSB).
contributions.detail: A more accurate map than Ptolemy's for Islamic lands according to DSB; unknown in Europe until the 19th century.
contributions.label: under_review

contributions.title: Mechanical devices (Kitab al-hiyal)
contributions.text: A work on mechanical devices attributed to the three brothers jointly; BEA says their mechanics marks significant advances over Philo of Byzantium and Hero of Alexandria. Device-level details need Hill's translation.
contributions.prior: The works of Philo and Hero, extensively known to Muslim engineers (BEA).
contributions.detail: BEA's judgement only; individual devices and inventors are not established from the sources read (popular claims are UNVERIFIED, B-12).
contributions.label: under_review

contributions.title: Book on the Measurement of Plane and Spherical Figures
contributions.text: A geometry treatise on measuring plane and spherical figures, attributed to the brothers jointly.
contributions.prior: Greek geometry, including Archimedes and Apollonius, available in Arabic (BEA mentions Apollonius in related works).
contributions.detail: BEA calls it one of the fundamental medieval geometry texts: recast by al-Tusi, translated by Gerard of Cremona, and reflected in later authors.
contributions.label: under_review

contributions.title: Sponsoring the acquisition and translation of classical works
contributions.text: The brothers funded the search for Greek manuscripts in Byzantium and employed translators, including Thabit ibn Qurra and Hunayn ibn Ishaq (per BEA).
contributions.prior: Greek scientific texts not yet in Arabic.
contributions.detail: BEA credits them with greatly promoting the translation movement; details on specific books are not given.
contributions.label: under_review

contributions.title: Critique of the Ptolemaic ninth sphere
contributions.text: Attributed to Muhammad: a book arguing that the daily motion of the heavens comes from rotation of all spheres, denying the ninth sphere that moves them in Ptolemy's scheme.
contributions.detail: A historical argument within Ptolemaic cosmology. Not a claim about modern astronomy (M-B1).
contributions.label: under_review

contributions.title: Geometric proof against a ninth sphere (reported)
contributions.text: Reportedly by Ahmad: a geometric demonstration that no sphere exists beyond the sphere of the fixed stars.
contributions.detail: Reported attribution only (BEA words it 'reportedly'); the text is not known to survive.
contributions.label: under_review

contributions.title: On First Philosophy: Greek arguments for a created world and a simple God
contributions.text: A treatise adapting Greek, especially Philoponus' and Neoplatonic, arguments to argue the world began and that God is a simple 'true One', dedicated to al-Mu'tasim.
contributions.prior: Aristotle, Neoplatonic texts and Philoponus' arguments against eternity (SEP).
contributions.detail: Presented as Arabic philosophy's first systematic metaphysics in SEP's characterisation (Q-15), but its argument for a beginning follows Philoponus.
contributions.label: under_review

contributions.title: Leading a translation circle
contributions.text: He led one of two main translation groups, whose output included the Theology of Aristotle and other Greek works, mediating between patrons and translators.
contributions.prior: Greek philosophy and science not yet in Arabic.
contributions.detail: The extent of his own translating versus organizing is not settled in the source ('seems to have been a mediator').
contributions.label: under_review

contributions.title: Geometric optics and critique of Euclid
contributions.text: Optical work (On Perspectives, Latin only) using geometry and the Euclid–Ptolemy tradition, including criticism of Euclid's theory of vision.
contributions.prior: Euclid's and Ptolemy's optics (vision by rays from the eye).
contributions.detail: Followed the emission model, later superseded; Ibn al-Haytham explained vision accurately some decades later (SEP).
contributions.label: under_review

contributions.title: On Rays (authenticity disputed)
contributions.text: A Latin-only treatise explaining physical and astral interaction by rays; its authorship is contested.
contributions.detail: SEP notes a strong case against his authorship (Matton 2022) while allowing it may rest on authentic material.
contributions.label: under_review

contributions.title: Collective scientific and translation patronage
contributions.text: Pingree and Casulleras describe the Banū Mūsā brothers collectively as patrons of scientific activity and translation in ninth-century Baghdad. The surviving record does not justify assigning every commission or translated work to a specific brother.
contributions.prior: Greek scientific works and Abbasid-era translation activity in Baghdad, as summarized by the cited scholars.
contributions.detail: A cautious group-level summary of modern academic biographies. Underlying Arabic notices and individual translator commissions still need direct source-level review.
contributions.label: under_review
